D.abstract.conclusion_sentence.value: In this synthesis of El Niño and health in India, no ENSO index was clearly preferred over the traditional ONI (pooled leave-one-El-Niño-out prediction error across 3 outcomes). For malaria, the ENSO-attributable out-of-sample log-score gain (observed ONI over a climatological ENSO value; positive = better) was −0.010 nats per unit-year (95% CI −0.020 to +0.001), not clearly different from zero. The observed-ONI model's gain over the no-ENSO comparison model (local climate, trend and programme terms and the lagged outcome) was −0.017 nats per unit-year (95% CI −0.041 to +0.007). For recorded heat deaths, the ENSO-attributable out-of-sample log-score gain was −0.002 nats per unit-year (95% CI −0.015 to +0.011), not clearly different from zero. The observed-ONI model's gain of +0.042 nats per unit-year (95% CI −0.021 to +0.104) over the no-ENSO comparison model is consistent with the non-ENSO Indian Ocean Dipole term that the model with ENSO terms also adds. State ranks on the El Niño Health Risk Index had a median 95% rank interval of 9 places across 32 ranked units and were broadly stable across weighting schemes (minimum Kendall τ 0.80).

D.ew.heat.note.value: For recorded heat deaths, a climatological ENSO value outperformed the observed ONI on average, though not clearly (−0.002 nats per unit-year; 95% CI −0.015 to +0.011). The gain of the model with ENSO terms over the model without them (+0.042 nats per unit-year with the observed ONI, +0.044 with a climatological value) is therefore not clearly attributable to the ENSO value (the 95% CI of the observed ONI's advantage over a climatological value reaches +0.011 nats per unit-year); it is consistent with the non-ENSO Indian Ocean Dipole term (September–November Dipole index) that the model also adds, although no model with the Dipole term and without the ENSO terms was fitted. Season-level gains with the observed ONI vary widely (SD 0.134 over 20 seasons); the two largest in absolute value, 2024 (+0.457) and 2020 (−0.311), account for most of that spread (87% of the squared deviations from the mean) rather than the mean, which is +0.038 without them. The June and September issues hold the September–November Dipole index and the lagged heat deaths at their observed values, which are not known at those issue times (the Dipole season is also incomplete at the November issue), so the forecast gains at those leads are not lead-time skill.

D.outlook.basis_text.value: The malaria layer is the projection of the companion state-panel malaria analysis at the provisional June–September 2026 traditional ONI of +1.78 °C and RONI of +1.34 °C (the mean of the May–July, June–August and July–September 2026 seasons; the August–October season had not been published). The heat layer gives the scenarios of the companion state-panel heat analysis for a December–February 2026–27 traditional ONI of +1.5, +2.0 and +2.5 °C, because that season had not been published; these values are scenarios and are provisional. Both layers give expected excess recorded counts under a common national El Niño association, distributed by each unit's baseline burden; they are model-based extrapolations, not state-specific sensitivities. ENSO values are those published up to the July–September 2026 season.

D.risk.AN.burden.description: Burden domain score of AN: mean of its components, each min-max scaled (0-1) across the ranked-eligible units (components of an NA-by-rule unit, AN or LD, clamped to [0, 1]); malaria API 3.53187 per 1,000 (23 years), dengue 43.4844 per 100,000 (19 years), heat deaths 0 per 10,000,000 (24 years), each scaled on log(1 + rate); stunting 22.5%, child anaemia 40% (NFHS-5); null if any component is NA
